#1
L: For my favor, the supreme secret called adhyātma — the word that was spoken by you — by that this delusion of mine is departed.
I: Out of kindness to me you have spoken the supreme secret teaching called adhyātma; through that teaching this confusion of mine has gone.
N: Chapter 11 opens with Arjuna speaking, thanking Kṛṣṇa for the teaching just given (chapters 2–10). Guhyam adhyātma-saṃjñitam, 'the secret called adhyātma', names that teaching by the technical term Kṛṣṇa himself used for it (adhyātma, 'pertaining to the self', defined at 8.3 as svabhāva, one's own essential nature); it is kept untranslated here as a named term, the way the poem's other technical words are. The sentence has no separate main verb: paramaṃ guhyam adhyātmasaṃjñitam all describe vacaḥ, 'the word', in apposition — 'the word, [namely] the supreme secret called adhyātma, which was spoken by you'. Two sandhis to notice: tat + śakyam-type -t + ś- patterns recur through the chapter (see v.4), and tvayā + uktam fuses to tvayoktam, -ā + u- → -o-, as at mohaḥ + ayam → moho'yam below (-aḥ + a- → -o with the avagraha marking the lost a-).
#2
L: The origin and passing-away indeed of beings have been heard by me in detail, and from you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, your imperishable greatness too.
I: I have already heard from you, in detail, of the birth and passing of all beings, and of your own greatness that never fades, lotus-eyed one.
N: Bhavāpyayau, 'origin-and-dissolution', is a dvandva (pair) compound in the dual, its two members glued together as one idea, the coming-to-be and passing-away of all beings — a theme Kṛṣṇa develops throughout chapters 7–10. Kamalapatrākṣa, 'lotus-petal-eyed', is an epithet of Kṛṣṇa; tvattaḥ, 'from you', is the ablative with the emphatic -tas suffix seen also in mattaḥ 'from me'. The second line's verb is understood by ellipsis: '[I have heard] your imperishable greatness too' repeats śrutau from the first line without restating it, a common economy in Sanskrit.
#3
L: So it is, as you have described yourself, O supreme lord; I wish to see your lordly form, O highest of beings.
I: It is just as you have described yourself, supreme lord — now I want to see that majestic form, highest of beings.
N: Āttha is an irregular perfect ('you have said'), from the defective root ah, which supplies only perfect-tense forms (āha 'he said' appeared throughout chapter 1). Parameśvara and puruṣottama are both vocatives addressed to Kṛṣṇa, 'supreme lord' and 'highest of persons' — titles that anticipate the vision to come. Rūpam aiśvaram, 'the lordly form', uses aiśvara, an adjective from īśvara 'lord', which recurs through the chapter (yogeśvara v.4, mahāyogeśvara v.9, yogam aiśvaram v.8) binding these opening verses together.
#4
L: If you think that it can be seen by me, O lord — then, O lord of yoga, show me your imperishable self.
I: If you think I am able to see it, Lord, then show me your imperishable self, lord of yoga.
N: Yogeśvara, 'lord of yoga', is Arjuna's climactic address, matched in v.9 when Sañjaya calls Kṛṣṇa mahāyogeśvaraḥ, 'the great lord of yoga', as he reveals the form. Tacchakyam is tat + śakyam, -t + ś- → -cch-, a sandhi that recurs at v.1's tatra note; śakyam is a gerundive, 'able to be done', used impersonally with an instrumental agent (mayā draṣṭum śakyam, 'it is possible for it to be seen by me' — i.e. 'I am able to see it'), the same construction returning as a personal passive in v.8's śakyase.
#5
L: Behold, O son of Pṛthā, my forms, by the hundreds and by the thousands — of many kinds, divine, of many colors and shapes.
I: Look, Arjuna, at my forms — hundreds of them, thousands of them, of every kind, divine, of every color and shape.
N: The Blessed Lord now answers, granting Arjuna's request. Śataśas and sahasraśas are distributive adverbs built with the suffix -śas, 'by the hundred', 'by the thousand' — the same formation as vistaraśaḥ in v.2. The compounds nānāvidha and nānāvarṇākṛti, 'of many kinds' and 'of many colors and shapes', both use nānā, 'various', which will recur as aneka, 'many, numerous', through the catalogue of verses 10–11.
#6
L: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts too; behold many wonders never seen before, O Bhārata.
I: Look at the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts as well; behold many marvels never seen before, Bhārata.
N: A roll-call of Vedic deity-classes: the twelve Ādityas (solar gods), the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twin Aśvins, and the storm-god Maruts — the standard thirty-three gods of the older pantheon, now subsumed into Kṛṣṇa's form. The whole string pañyādityānvasūnrudrānaśvinau is one written word only because each accusative ends in a consonant that joins directly to the next; the reading separates the five names. Bhārata, 'descendant of Bharata', here addresses Arjuna (in chapter 1 the same title was for Dhṛtarāṣṭra) — both houses descend from Bharata.
#7
L: Here, united in one place, behold today the whole world, moving and unmoving together, in my body, O lord of sleep — and whatever else you wish to see.
I: Here in my body, Arjuna, see today the whole universe gathered into one place, everything that moves and everything that does not — and whatever else you want to see.
N: Sacarācaram, 'with the moving and the unmoving', is a standard Sanskrit pair for 'everything animate and inanimate', built from cara 'moving' and its negation acara. Guḍākeśa, 'thick-haired' or, by another reading, 'conqueror of sleep', is the same epithet of Arjuna used at 1.24. Yaccānyad is a triple sandhi worth tracing: yat + ca → yac ca (-t + c- → -c c-), then ca + anyat → cānyat (a + a → ā), and the final -t of anyat surfaces as -d before the voiced d- of draṣṭum that follows.
#8
L: But you cannot see me with this eye of your own; I give you a divine eye — behold my lordly yoga.
I: But you cannot see me with your own eyes as they are. I will give you a divine eye — now see my majestic power.
N: Śakyase is the personal-passive use of the gerundive śak(ya) with an infinitive: not 'you can be seen' but 'you are able [to see]', the construction already used impersonally at v.4. The divya cakṣus, 'divine eye', that Kṛṣṇa now grants is the device that makes the whole vision possible — Arjuna's ordinary sight cannot bear it. Yogam aiśvaram, 'majestic yoga' or 'the yoga-power of lordship', names what Arjuna is about to see: not a static form but Kṛṣṇa's own divine capacity in action.
#9
L: Having thus spoken, then, O king, Hari, the great lord of yoga, showed to the son of Pṛthā his supreme lordly form.
N: Sañjaya resumes the narration, addressing the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra as rājan, 'O king'. Hari, 'the tawny one', is a name of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; mahāyogeśvaraḥ, 'the great lord of yoga', answers Arjuna's own address yogeśvara in v.4. Darśayām āsa is a periphrastic perfect, a formation classical Sanskrit uses for certain derived and causative verbs in place of a simple reduplicated perfect.
#10
L: Of many mouths and eyes, of many marvelous aspects, of many divine ornaments, with many divine weapons raised —
I: with countless mouths and eyes, countless wonders to see, countless divine ornaments, and countless divine weapons raised —
N: This verse and the next are a chain of bahuvrīhi compounds — 'possessive' compounds naming the form by what it has, all in the accusative describing rūpam from v.9 — with no finite verb of their own; the sentence is completed only in v.13's apaśyat, 'he saw'. Each pair of compounds is joined by the same word aneka, 'many, numerous', repeated four times across the two verses, mounting the sense of overwhelming multiplicity.
#11
L: wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with divine fragrance — the god all-wondrous, infinite, facing every way.
I: wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with heavenly fragrance — a god of every wonder, without end, facing every direction.
N: The chain of compounds from v.10 concludes here on devam, 'the god' — the grammatical head that all of vv.10–11 have been describing. Viśvatomukham, 'facing every way', is a celebrated old epithet (compare the Vedic viśvataścakṣuḥ, 'eyed on every side'), later echoed at 13.13. Sarvāścaryamayam, 'made wholly of wonder', uses the suffix -maya, '(consisting) of, full of' — the same suffix that will form nāmarūpamaya-type compounds elsewhere in Sanskrit philosophical writing.
#12
L: If in the sky the light of a thousand suns should rise up at once, that would be like the splendor of that great-souled one.
I: If a thousand suns were to blaze up together in the sky, their light would still be no more than a match for the splendor of that great being.
N: One of the poem's most quoted images. Bhavet and syāt are both optative, 'were to be' / 'would be', framing a contrary-to-fact comparison: 'if X were to happen, Y would be [merely] like it'. Mahātman, 'great-souled', a standard honorific compound (mahā + ātman), here names the being whose splendor exceeds even that thousand-sun light — Kṛṣṇa in his cosmic form. Note the run of sandhi: bhavet + yugapat → bhaved yugapat (-t + y- → -d y-), yugapat + utthitā → yugapad utthitā (-t + u- → -d u-), syāt + bhāsaḥ → syād bhāsaḥ (-t + bh- → -d bh-), bhāsaḥ + tasya → bhāsas tasya (-aḥ + t- → -as t-).
#13
L: There, united in one, the whole world divided in many ways, the Pāṇḍava then saw, in the body of the god of gods.
I: There, in the body of the god of gods, Arjuna then saw the whole universe gathered into one, divided in countless ways.
N: This verse finally supplies the finite verb, apaśyat, 'he saw', that the long descriptive sentence of vv.9–11 has been waiting for: what Kṛṣṇa showed, Arjuna now sees. Deva-deva, 'the god of gods', is the poem's title for Kṛṣṇa's cosmic form. Eka-stham ... anekadhā, 'united in one ... divided in many ways', sets side by side the paradox at the heart of the vision — the whole universe is at once one thing and countless things.
#14
L: Then he, overcome with astonishment, his hair bristling, Dhanañjaya — having bowed his head to the god, with hands folded, spoke.
I: Then Arjuna, overwhelmed with wonder, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god and, hands folded, began to speak.
N: Vismayāviṣṭaḥ, 'entered by astonishment', uses ā-viś, 'to enter, possess', the same verb that described Arjuna being overcome by pity at 1.28 (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ); hṛṣṭaromā, 'hair bristling', echoes the shock-symptoms of 1.29 (romaharṣa, 'hair-thrill'), though there from dread and here from awe. Añjali, the cupped-hands gesture of reverence, marks the shift from Sañjaya's narration into the hymn of praise (the Viśvarūpa-stuti) that follows in the verses beyond this chunk. Dhanaṃjaya, 'winner of wealth', Arjuna's title, is spelled here with anusvāra for the class nasal — an orthographic variant, not a real one, and needs no correction note.
#15
L: I see the gods, O God, in your body, and likewise all the hosts of the various kinds of beings; Brahmā the lord seated-on-the-lotus-seat, and the sages, and all the divine serpents.
I: In your body I see the gods, O God, and with them the hosts of every kind of being; Brahmā the creator seated on his lotus, the sages, and all the divine serpents.
N: This is the chapter's first triṣṭubh (four-line, eleven-syllable) verse; from here through the rest of Arjuna's speech the grander triṣṭubh replaces the śloka couplets used earlier in the chapter. The Wikisource print breaks the compound kamalāsana-stham, 'seated on the lotus-seat' (describing Brahmā), oddly across the pāda boundary: कमलासनस्थ- ends line 3 and the bare म् completing it opens line 4 before ऋषींश्च; the two are drafted as separate words-entries only to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split. Brahmā, born on a lotus from Viṣṇu's navel in the epic cosmology, is named here alongside the sages and the divine serpents (nāgas) as inhabitants of the cosmic form, signalling that the whole created order is visible within it.
#16
L: Many-armed-bellied-mouthed-eyed, I see you, on-every-side of-infinite-form; no end, no middle, nor again your beginning do I see, O Lord-of-the-universe, universal-formed one.
I: I see you with countless arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, your form without end on every side; I find no end, no middle, and no beginning in you, Lord of the universe, you whose very form is the universe.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ. The compound anekabāhūdaravaktranetram, 'having many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes', undoes at the hyphen the vowel fusion bāhu + udara → bāhūdara. Viśveśvara ('Lord of the universe') and viśvarūpa ('having the universe as your form') are the two vocatives that name this chapter's vision; the second gives the chapter its title, Viśvarūpadarśana.
#17
L: Crowned, mace-bearing, discus-bearing, a mass-of-radiance blazing on every side, I see you, hard-to-behold, on-all-sides blazing-with-the-light-of-fire-and-sun, immeasurable.
I: I see you crowned, bearing mace and discus, a mass of light blazing on every side, hard to look at, ablaze all around like fire and sun, beyond all measure.
N: The Wikisource print breaks the phrase samantāt dīptānalārkadyutim, '[blazing] on all sides with the light of fire and sun', across the pāda boundary: समन्ता- ends line 3, dropping the word's final -t; that -t resurfaces, voiced to -d by sandhi before the following d-, as the bare द् that opens line 4's द्दीप्तानलार्कद्युतिमप्रमेयम्. Drafted as two words-entries to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split (cf. verse 15 above). Kirīṭin, gadin, cakrin are all -in possessive formations, 'crown-having', 'mace-having', 'discus-having' — three of Viṣṇu's traditional emblems (the fourth, the lotus, is not named here).
#18
L: You are the Imperishable, the supreme thing-to-be-known; you are of this universe the supreme resting-place; you are imperishable, the guardian of eternal-dharma; the eternal one, you, the Person, are thought by me.
I: You are the Imperishable, the highest object of knowledge. You are the ultimate resting-place of this whole universe. You are the undying guardian of eternal dharma. You are, I believe, the eternal, primeval Person.
N: Four parallel tvam-clauses (tvam akṣaram, tvam asya ... parama nidhānam, tvam avyayaḥ, sanātanas tvam) name Kṛṣṇa with a string of philosophical titles: akṣara, 'the Imperishable', is a standard Upaniṣadic name for the changeless absolute; puruṣa, 'the Person', is the term Sāṃkhya uses for the ultimate self, here identified with Kṛṣṇa outright. Dharma in śāśvata-dharma-goptā is the cosmic order in the general sense (left untranslated per house style), not any one family's custom, as elsewhere in the poem. Mato me, 'thought by me', is a past participle with its agent in the instrumental — the ordinary Sanskrit way of saying 'I think, in my view'.
#19
L: Without-beginning-middle-end, of-infinite-power, infinite-armed, moon-and-sun-eyed, I see you, blazing-fire-mouthed, with-your-own-radiance scorching this universe.
I: I see you without beginning, middle, or end, your power boundless, your arms without number, the sun and moon your eyes; your mouth ablaze like fire, scorching this whole universe with your own radiance.
N: The Wikisource print breaks anantavīryam, 'of infinite power', across the pāda boundary, printing अनादिमध्यान्तमनन्तवीर्य- at the end of line 1 and completing it with a bare म् at the start of line 2 before अनन्तबाहुं; here the leftover म् simply attaches to the following vowel-initial word with no further sandhi change. Drafted as two words-entries to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split (cf. verses 15 and 17 above). An-ādi-madhya-anta is a four-member bahuvrīhi, 'having no beginning, middle, or end'; hutāśa, literally 'oblation-eater', is an old epithet of Agni, fire, used here as a plain word for fire itself.
#20
L: This the-space-between-heaven-and-earth indeed is pervaded by-you-alone, and the-directions, all of them; having-seen this wonderful, terrible form of-yours, the-triple-world trembles, O great-souled one.
I: This space between heaven and earth, and all the directions besides, are filled by you alone. Having seen this astonishing, terrible form of yours, the three worlds tremble, great soul.
N: BORI reads rūpam idaṃ tavograṃ (transposing idam and ugram/tava) for the vulgate's rūpam ugraṃ tavedaṃ; the sense is unchanged. Dyāvāpṛthivī, 'heaven-and-earth', is a fixed Vedic dvandva compound, always dual; its whole space (antaram) is said to be filled by Kṛṣṇa's form alone. Mahātman, 'great-souled', addresses Kṛṣṇa directly for the first time in this vision, a title the poem elsewhere also gives to sages and heroes.
#21
L: These hosts-of-gods indeed enter you; some, frightened, hands-folded, cry-out; having-said 'Hail!', the-hosts-of-great-sages-and-perfected-beings praise you with-abundant hymns-of-praise.
I: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, terrified, cry out with hands folded in reverence; the hosts of great sages and perfected beings, crying 'Hail!', praise you with abundant hymns.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ. Amī, 'those, these', is the nominative plural of the distal demonstrative adas, referring here to the gods now visible entering Kṛṣṇa's gaping mouths, an image the chapter develops further in the verses that follow this excerpt. Svastīty uktvā, 'having said svasti', is the standard Vedic blessing-cry, 'hail! all is well!', cried out by the sages and perfected beings at the terrifying sight.
#22
L: The-Rudras-and-Ādityas, the Vasus, and whichever Sādhyas there are; the-Viśvedevas, the-two-Aśvins, the Maruts and the-steam-drinking-ancestors, and the-hosts-of-gandharvas-yakṣas-asuras-and-siddhas — they gaze-at you, astonished, all indeed.
I: The Rudras and Ādityas, the Vasus, and whatever Sādhyas there are; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the ancestral spirits who feed on the sacrificial steam; the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and siddhas — all of them stare at you, astonished.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ, in vīkṣante tvāṃ. The verse rolls out the classes of Vedic gods: the eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, eight Vasus, the Sādhyas and Viśvedevas (minor divine classes), the twin horsemen Aśvins, the storm-gods Maruts, and the uṣmapāḥ, 'steam-drinkers' — an epithet of the Pitṛs, the ancestral spirits, who partake of the rising heat of the offerings. Alongside them stand gandharvas (celestial musicians), yakṣas (nature-spirits), asuras (demons) and siddhas (perfected beings): every order of being in the traditional cosmos, all astonished at once.
#23
L: Your great form, many-mouthed-and-eyed, O mighty-armed one, many-armed-thighed-and-footed, many-bellied, terrible-with-many-fangs — having seen it, the worlds tremble, and so do I.
I: Seeing your vast form, mighty-armed one, with its many mouths and eyes, its many arms, thighs, and feet, its many bellies and its rows of terrible fangs, the worlds tremble — and so do I.
N: Mahābāho, 'mighty-armed', addresses Kṛṣṇa even as Arjuna describes the terror of what he sees — an epithet more often given to warriors, turned here onto the god in his monstrous form. Bahu-bāhu-ūru-pādam undoes the vowel fusion bāhu + ūru → bāhūru at the hyphen, and bahūdaram undoes bahu + udara → bahūdara the same way. Tathāham, 'and so I too', ends the verse: even Arjuna, who asked to see this form, is now as shaken as the onlooking worlds.
#24
L: Sky-touching, blazing, many-colored, mouth-gaping-wide, blazing-vast-eyed — having-seen you indeed, my-inner-self-trembling, steadiness I do not find, nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
I: Touching the sky, blazing, many-colored, your mouth wide open, your eyes huge and blazing — having seen you, my innermost self trembles; I can find no steadiness, no peace, Viṣṇu.
N: Viṣṇu, kept untranslated as the proper name it is, appears here for the first time in this vision as a name addressed to Kṛṣṇa, identifying him outright with the great preserver-god of the classical triad. Nabhaḥ-spṛśam, 'touching the sky', keeps its visarga unchanged before the following voiceless s-. The compound pravyathita-antar-ātmā, 'whose inmost self is trembling', names Arjuna's own state, not Kṛṣṇa's: the subject shifts here from the 'you' of the first two lines to the 'I' who is speaking.
#25
L: Fang-terrible your mouths, having-seen indeed, resembling-the-fire-of-doomsday — the directions I know not, nor do I find peace; be gracious, O lord-of-gods, abode-of-the-universe.
I: Seeing your mouths, terrible with fangs, like the fires that end the world, I lose all sense of direction and find no peace. Have mercy, lord of the gods, abode of the universe!
N: Daṃṣṭrā-karālāni ('terrible with fangs') and kāla-analasannibhāni ('resembling the fire of doomsday') both describe mukhāni, the object of dṛṣṭvā; kālānala, 'the fire of Time', is the conflagration that ends each cosmic age — the same kāla that names itself outright in verse 32. Arjuna's speech, begun at v.15, continues uninterrupted through v.31. Deveśa and jagannivāsa are two vocatives addressed to the cosmic form: 'lord of the gods' and 'abode of the universe' (jagat + nivāsa, -t + n- → -n n-).
#26
L: And these, you — the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of them, together indeed with hosts-of-kings; Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the charioteer's-son likewise, he too, together with our own chief-warriors too —
I: And these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of them, together with hosts of kings, rush toward you — Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Karṇa the charioteer's son too, together with our own chief warriors —
N: Verses 26–27 are a single sentence: the subject amī ... putrāḥ ... sarve, 'these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of them', with the list of named warriors here, and the verb viśanti, 'they enter', arriving only in v.27. Tvām, accusative, anticipates that verb and is resumed there by vaktrāṇi te, 'your mouths' — 'they enter you, [namely] your mouths'. Sūtaputra, 'the charioteer's son', names Karṇa without naming him, the epic's usual discretion about his birth.
#27
L: Your mouths, hastening, they enter, fang-terrible, frightful; some, stuck between the teeth, are seen with heads crushed.
I: They rush headlong into your mouths, terrible with fangs, dreadful to see; some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads already crushed.
N: Completes the sentence begun in v.26: subject amī ... putrāḥ ... sarve, verb viśanti, object vaktrāṇi te. Daṃṣṭrā-karālāni repeats the phrase from v.25, now describing the mouths directly instead of through a gerund. Uttamāṅga, 'the highest limb', is a standard periphrasis for 'the head'.
#28
L: As of rivers many water-currents toward the ocean indeed, facing-onward, flow, so these heroes-of-the-human-world your mouths enter, blazing-fiercely.
I: As many rushing currents of rivers race straight toward the ocean, so these heroes of the human world rush into your fiercely blazing mouths.
N: The first of two explicit similes (yathā ... tathā) describing warriors rushing to their deaths; v.29 repeats the pattern with moths and a flame. Vaktrāṇi does double duty, as object of viśanti and subject of abhivijvalanti, a compression typical of the verse's headlong pace.
#29
L: As, into a blazing flame, moths enter to their destruction, with gathered-speed, so too, to destruction, the-worlds enter your mouths as well, with gathered-speed.
I: As moths, with mounting speed, fly into a blazing flame to their doom, so too, with mounting speed, these people rush to their doom in your mouths.
N: A hyphen split across the pāda boundary: the sandhi lokāḥ + tava → lokās tava is printed split by Wikisource as लोका- at the end of the third line and स्तवापि at the start of the fourth; the leftover स् that opens स्तवापि completes लोकाः, drafted here as two words-entries only to tile the source exactly, on the model of ch09 v.20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split. Samṛddhavegāḥ, 'with gathered speed', is used twice, first of the moths, then of the doomed people, tying the simile tightly to its object.
#30
L: You lick-up, devouring, from-all-sides all the worlds with mouths blazing; having filled with your radiances the whole universe, your splendors, fierce, blaze-forth, O Viṣṇu.
I: You lick them up, devouring, swallowing all the worlds from every side with your blazing mouths; filling the whole universe with your radiance, your fierce splendors burn everywhere, Viṣṇu.
N: Another hyphen split, on the same model as v.29: samantāt + lokān → samantāl lokān is printed समन्ता- at the end of the first line and ल्लोकान्समग्रान्वदनैर्ज्वलद्भिः at the start of the second, the leftover ल् beginning the second line's token. Viṣṇo is the first point in the whole vision where Arjuna names the cosmic form outright as Viṣṇu.
#31
L: Tell me who you are, of fierce-form; homage be to you, O best-of-gods, be gracious. I wish to know fully you, the primal one; for I do not understand your course-of-action.
I: Tell me who you are, in this terrible form. Homage to you, best of gods — have mercy! I want to understand you, the primal being; I cannot fathom what you are doing.
N: Closes Arjuna's speech (begun at v.15) with a direct question, answered at once in v.32. Pravṛtti, 'activity, course, function', is broad — what the form is doing, and to what end.
#32
L: Time I am, world-destruction-making, grown-great, here set-in-motion to gather in the worlds; even without you, all these warriors standing in the opposing ranks will not be.
I: I am Time, grown vast, the wrecker of worlds, at work here to gather the worlds in. Even without you, none of the warriors drawn up in the facing lines will survive.
N: The pivot of the chapter: kāla is Time itself — the impersonal power that both generates and dissolves the worlds — not 'Death', the famous rendering this drafting does not follow. Pravṛddhaḥ ('grown vast') and pravṛttaḥ ('now at work'), both nominative in apposition to kālaḥ, present Time as already immense and already in motion; lokān samāhartum, 'to gather in the worlds', casts the destruction as a harvest rather than a slaughter. Ṛte governs the accusative tvām, 'apart from you', the same construction found elsewhere in this chapter (vv.16, 20–22). BORI reads tvā (enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ.
#33
L: Therefore, you, arise, win fame; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a flourishing kingdom. By me indeed already these have been slain, beforehand; be a mere instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
I: So rise up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a flourishing kingdom. I myself have already slain them, beforehand; be merely my instrument, Savyasācin.
N: Nimitta-mātram, 'a mere occasion, a mere instrument', is the verse's famous phrase: Arjuna is not the true agent of the killing, already accomplished by kāla, but only its visible means. Savyasācin, 'able to shoot with the left hand too', names Arjuna's ambidexterity as a warrior.
#34
L: Droṇa and Bhīṣma and Jayadratha and Karṇa, and likewise other warrior-heroes too — slain already by me, you, kill! Do not waver; fight — a conqueror you are, in battle, over your rivals.
I: Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the other warrior-heroes too — they are already slain by me; you need only strike them down. Do not waver — fight! You will be victorious over your rivals in battle.
N: Continues v.33's teaching with a list of the very men Arjuna most dreads killing, all declared already slain. Jetāsi, 'you are a conqueror', a present-tense statement of a settled future, echoes kāla's claim in v.32 that the outcome is already fixed. Mā vyathiṣṭhāḥ, 'do not waver', is a prohibitive with the aorist injunctive, the mood regularly used with mā.
#35
L: This word of the slayer-of-Keśin having-heard, with-folded-hands, trembling, the-crowned-one, having-done-homage, again indeed spoke to Kṛṣṇa — brokenly, frightened-again-and-again, having-prostrated.
I: Sañjaya said: Hearing this from Keśava, Arjuna, the crowned one, folded his hands and, trembling, bowed low; then, his voice breaking, utterly afraid, he prostrated himself and spoke again to Kṛṣṇa.
N: The whole verse is one sentence, still narrated by Sañjaya: a chain of participles and gerunds (kṛtāñjaliḥ 'with folded hands', vepamānaḥ 'trembling', namaskṛtvā 'having bowed', bhīta-bhītaḥ 'utterly afraid', praṇamya 'having prostrated') built around the single finite verb āha, 'he spoke'. Kirīṭī, 'the crowned one' — from the diadem Indra gave him — and Keśava, 'having fine hair' or 'slayer of the demon Keśin', are epithets of Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa respectively. Sandhi: एतच्छ्रुत्वा is etat + śrutvā (-t + ś- → -c ch-); कृताञ्जलिर्वेपमानः is kṛtāñjaliḥ + vepamānaḥ (-iḥ + v- → -ir v-); भूय एवाह shows bhūyaḥ losing its visarga entirely before the vowel e- of eva — before a non-a vowel a final -aḥ simply drops, with no -o and no avagraha, unlike before a- — and then eva + āha: a + ā → ā.
#36
L: Fitting it is, O lord-of-the-senses, at-your renown, the-world rejoices and-becomes-delighted; the-demons, frightened, to-the-directions flee; all indeed pay-homage, and the-hosts-of-siddhas.
I: Arjuna said: It is fitting, Hṛṣīkeśa, that at your renown the world rejoices and is filled with delight; the demons, terrified, flee in every direction; and all the hosts of the perfected ones bow down.
N: Sthāne is an adverbial idiom, 'fittingly, it stands to reason', not a literal 'in the place'; this opens Arjuna's hymn of praise (stuti) that runs through the rest of the chapter. Rakṣāṃsi, 'rākṣasas, demons', flee in terror while the siddhas, 'perfected, accomplished beings' (a class of minor divinities), bow down — the universal awe Sañjaya has just narrated from the outside is now Arjuna's own theme. Sandhi: जगत्प्रहृष्यत्यनुरज्यते packs jagat + prahṛṣyati (simply written joined, no phonetic change) + prahṛṣyati + anurajyate (-i + a- → -y a-); दिशो is diśaḥ, -aḥ before d- → -o.
#37
L: And-why should-they not bow to-you, O great-souled-one, greater even-than Brahmā, the-original-creator; O endless-one, O lord-of-gods, O abode-of-the-universe — you are the-imperishable, being-and-non-being, and what is beyond-that.
I: And why should they not bow to you, great one — you who are greater even than Brahmā, the first creator? Endless one, lord of the gods, dwelling-place of the universe: you are the imperishable — being and non-being, and what lies beyond both.
N: ब्रह्मणः here names the god Brahmā, the creator (an ablative of comparison with garīyase, 'greater than Brahmā'): a proper name, not the abstract, untranslated brahman of the conventions. The context — 'greater even than Brahmā, the original creator [ādikartre]' — makes plain this is the personal creator-god, one figure among those Kṛṣṇa is said to surpass, not the impersonal absolute; it is capitalized and translated as a name accordingly. Akṣaram, sad-asat, tat param, and the closing yat build the same formula found at 13.12 and echoed elsewhere in the poem: the imperishable is what is 'being and non-being, and what is beyond both'. Sandhi: कस्माच्च is kasmāt + ca (-t + c- → -c c-); नमेरन्महात्मन् simply writes nameran + mahātman joined, with no phonetic change, as consonant-final words are often printed in this text; ब्रह्मणोऽप्यादिकर्त्रे packs brahmaṇaḥ + api (-aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha) + api + ādikartre (-i + ā- → -y ā-); जगन्निवास is jagat + nivāsa (-t + n- → -n n-); सदसत्तत्परं packs sat + asat (-t + a- → -d a-) + asat + tat (-t + t- → -t t-, written doubled).
#38
L: You are the-primal-god, the-Person, the-ancient-one; you are of-this universe the-supreme resting-place. You are the-knower and the-knowable, and the-supreme abode; by-you is pervaded the-universe, O-one-of-infinite-form.
I: You are the primal god, the ancient Person; you are the supreme resting-place of this universe. You are the knower and the known, and the highest abode; by you this whole universe is pervaded, boundless in form.
N: The Wikisource print line breaks the word पुराणस्त्वम् (purāṇaḥ + tvam, 'you are ancient') exactly at the pāda boundary, into पुराण- and स्त्वमस्य; the two are one continuous phrase — purāṇaḥ (nom. sg., predicate) + tvam asya ('you, of this [universe]') — with the visarga of purāṇaḥ turning to -s- before the following t-, and are drafted here as two words-entries only to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's sura-indra-lokam/aśnanti split. Puruṣa, the cosmic Person or Spirit set against prakṛti ('nature') in the Sāṃkhya scheme, is translated here as 'the Person' rather than left untranslated, since it is not among the terms the conventions single out (dharma, yoga, brahman, the guṇas, sāṃkhya). Vettā...vedyam plays on the root vid, 'to know': Kṛṣṇa is named both the knower and the known. Sandhi: वेत्तासि is vettā + asi (ā + a → ā).
#39
L: Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the-moon; Prajāpati are you, and the-great-grandfather too. Homage, homage to-you be — a-thousand-times; and-again and yet-again, homage, homage to-you!
I: You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon; you are Prajāpati, and the great-grandfather beyond him. Homage to you, homage, a thousand times over — and again, and yet again, homage, homage to you!
N: A catalogue verse identifying Kṛṣṇa with the great gods of the Vedic pantheon — Vāyu (wind), Yama (death), Agni (fire), Varuṇa (the waters), the moon, Prajāpati ('lord of creatures', a creator-deity) — and then with prapitāmaha, 'the great-grandfather', one step beyond even Brahmā, the grandfather-creator named in the previous verse. The second half is a chant of repeated prostration, namo namas te...namo namas te, 'homage, homage to you', doubled for intensity and repeated a second time. Sandhi: वायुर्यमोऽग्निर्वरुणः packs vāyuḥ + yamaḥ (-uḥ + y- → -ur y-) + yamaḥ + agniḥ (-aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha) + agniḥ + varuṇaḥ (-iḥ + v- → -ir v-); प्रजापतिस्त्वं is prajāpatiḥ + tvam (-iḥ + t- → -is t-, visarga before a voiceless consonant); नमस्तेऽस्तु packs namaḥ + te (-aḥ + t- → -as t-) + te + astu (-e + a- → -e ' with avagraha, as at ch01 33's ta ime 'vasthitāḥ); सर्वत (verse 40) drops its visarga entirely before eva, the same non-a-vowel rule as verse 35's bhūya eva.
#40
L: Homage in-front, and-then from-behind to-you; homage be to-you from-every-side indeed, O-All! Of-endless-might-and-immeasurable-prowess are you; everything you-pervade, therefore you-are all.
I: Homage to you from in front, and homage from behind; homage to you from every side, O you who are all! You are of boundless might and measureless prowess; you pervade everything, and so you are everything.
N: The prostration of verse 39 continues from every direction — front, back, every side — and the verse closes on a wordplay: sarva, 'all', names Kṛṣṇa as the universal being who samāpnoṣi, 'pervades, fully comprehends', sarvam, 'everything', and so tataḥ, 'therefore', asi sarvaḥ, 'you are all'. Sandhi: पुरस्तादथ is purastāt + atha (-t + a- → -d a-); पृष्ठतस्ते is pṛṣṭhataḥ + te (-aḥ + t- → -as t-); नमोऽस्तु and ततोऽसि both show -aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha; अनन्तवीर्यामितविक्रमस्त्वं packs vīrya + amita (a + a → ā) and the compound's own visarga + tvam (-aḥ + t- → -as t-).
#41
L: Thinking [you] 'a friend', whatever presumptuously was said — 'Hey Kṛṣṇa, hey Yādava, hey friend!' — by me, not knowing this greatness of yours, out of carelessness or out of affection —
I: Thinking of you only as a friend, and not knowing this greatness of yours, whatever I carelessly said — or said out of affection — 'Hey Kṛṣṇa! Hey Yādava! Hey friend!' —
N: Verses 41–44 are one long sentence, built on a relative-correlative pair spread across four verses: yad uktam here in the first line ('whatever was said') and yac cāvahāsārtham asatkṛto 'si in 42.1 ('and whatever disrespect you suffered in jest') are both picked up by the two instances of tat in 42.4 (tatsamakṣam, tatkṣāmaye, 'in [your/their] presence... for that I ask forgiveness'). This verse itself has no finite verb; it is the first half of that suspended clause, continued in 42. Note sakheti twice: sakhā + iti, 'thinking "a friend"' and, closing the quoted greeting, '"...a friend!"' — the same fusion, -ā + i- → -e-, seen throughout the chapter (cf. 1.1 pāṇḍavāś caiva). Ajānatā (line 3) and mayā (line 4) are separated by the line break but form one phrase, 'by me, not knowing'; Sanskrit lets an adjective and the noun it modifies fall on either side of an intervening word or line. Yādava, 'descendant of Yadu', is another name for Kṛṣṇa, born into the Yadu clan.
#42
L: And whatever, for the sake of a joke, you were treated disrespectfully — in play, in bed, at the seat, or at meals, — whether alone, O Unshakeable one, or also in [their] presence — for that I ask you, the immeasurable one, to forgive [me].
I: and for whatever disrespect I showed you in jest — at play, in bed, at table, sitting together — whether we were alone, Acyuta, or in company, I ask you, the immeasurable one, to forgive it all.
N: The correlative begun in 41 (yad uktam...) resolves here: tatsamakṣam and tatkṣāmaye both use tat, but to different ends — the first is an adverbial compound, tat-samakṣam, 'in that [company's] presence, openly' (paired with ekaḥ, 'alone', to mean 'whether privately or in front of others'), the second is the plain accusative object of kṣāmaye, 'I ask pardon for that [whole list of offenses]'. Two long lines are single unbroken tokens on Wikisource because they carry no internal word-breaking sandhi that would otherwise split them onto separate print words: yac cāvahāsārthamasatkṛto 'si strings together yat, ca, avahāsārtham ('for the sake of a joke') and asatkṛto 'si ('you were treated improperly'); vihāraśayyāsanabhojaneṣu lists, in one locative plural compound, the settings — play, rest, sitting, meals. Acyuta, 'the Unfallen', is an epithet of Kṛṣṇa. Kṣāmaye is a causative from kṣam 'to forgive, be patient' used in the sense 'I beg to be forgiven, I crave pardon'.
#43
L: You are the father of the world, of the moving and the unmoving; you are its one-to-be-honored and its more-venerable teacher; there is not one equal to you — how then another surpassing [you] — even in the three worlds, O one of unequalled majesty.
I: You are the father of this whole world, of everything that moves and everything that does not; you are its object of reverence and its teacher, greater than any. No one equals you — let alone surpasses you — in all three worlds, you whose majesty has no parallel.
N: Cara-acara, 'moving and unmoving', is the standard Sanskrit merism for 'everything that lives and everything that does not' — the whole created world. The verse builds a small climax: na tvatsamaḥ, 'not your equal'; kuto 'nyo 'bhyadhikaḥ, 'how [could there be] another surpassing [you]' — 'not even your equal, let alone your better'. Loka-traya, 'the triple world', is the traditional three: heaven, earth, and the netherworld (or, in some readings, heaven, earth, and the middle atmosphere). Guru, 'teacher', takes its own comparative form garīyān, 'weightier, more venerable' — an ordinary Sanskrit pattern, an adjective compared by a separate comparative stem rather than a suffix on itself.
#44
L: Therefore, having bowed, having prostrated [my] body, I seek to win your favor, [you] the lord, worthy of praise; as a father [bears] with a son, as a friend with a friend, as a lover with the beloved, you ought, O God, to bear [with me].
I: So I bow down, I prostrate my whole body, and beg your favor, lord, worthy of every praise. The way a father overlooks a son's faults, a friend a friend's, a lover the beloved's — so you, God, should overlook mine.
N: The three comparisons — pitā iva putrasya, sakhā iva sakhyuḥ, priyaḥ priyāyāḥ — share a single verb, stated only once at the end: arhasi...soḍhum, 'you ought to bear/endure'. Sanskrit regularly compresses parallel clauses this way, letting one verb serve all three. The third pair shifts register: priyaḥ (masc. nom.) and priyāyāḥ (fem. gen.) are 'the [male] beloved' and 'the [female] beloved' — a lover and his beloved — moving the image from father and friend to something more intimate. Praṇamya and praṇidhāya kāyam both describe the same physical prostration, first the general gesture then specifically 'the body' laid down.
#45
L: Having seen [what was] never-seen-before, I am thrilled; and by fear my mind is agitated. That very [form] show me again, O God; be gracious, O lord-of-gods, O abode-of-the-universe.
I: Having seen what no one has ever seen before, I am overjoyed, but my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that very form again, God; have mercy, lord of the gods, abode of the universe.
N: Adṛṣṭa-pūrvam, 'not-seen-before', is a common idiom compound: a past participle plus pūrva, 'earlier', meaning 'never before [done]'. The line pairs two opposite feelings in one breath, hṛṣita ('thrilled, bristling with joy') and pravyathita ('shaken, agitated') — Arjuna's vision of the cosmic form in the preceding verses has overwhelmed him with both wonder and terror, and this verse begins his plea to see the gentler form again, completed in 46. Manaḥ shows the ordinary visarga sandhi -aḥ becoming -o before a following voiced consonant (mano me), distinct from the -aḥ + vowel → -o + avagraha pattern seen earlier in this chapter. Deveśa (deva + īśa, 'lord of the gods') and jagannivāsa ('abode of the universe', jagat + nivāsa, with -t assimilating to -n before n-) are both vocatives addressing Kṛṣṇa.
#46
L: Crowned, mace-bearing, disc-in-hand — I wish to see you, thus indeed; with that very form, four-armed, O thousand-armed one, become [it], O universal-formed one.
I: I want to see you as before — with your diadem, your mace, the discus in your hand — in that same four-armed form; become that, thousand-armed one, universal-formed one.
N: The Wikisource print breaks the compound cakra-hastam ('having the disc in hand') across the line, giving चक्रहस्त- at the end of line 1 and मिच्छामि, 'm' + icchāmi, at the start of line 2 — the leftover final -m of hastam simply begins the next printed word. This is drafted as two words-entries only to tile the source exactly, on the model of ch09 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split. Kirīṭin, gadin, and cakra-hasta name the familiar four-armed icon of Viṣṇu — diadem, mace, and discus — the form Arjuna knew before this chapter's terrifying vision, and asks to see again in place of it. The closing address is pointed: Arjuna calls Kṛṣṇa sahasra-bāho, 'thousand-armed', and viśva-mūrte, 'universal-formed' — the very titles of the form that has frightened him — while begging him to 'become' (bhava) the smaller, four-armed shape instead.
#47
L: By me, gracious, this supreme form has been shown to you, Arjuna, through my own power of yoga: blazing, universal, endless, primal — which, by anyone other than you, has never before been seen.
I: Pleased with you, Arjuna, I have shown you, through my own yogic power, this supreme form — blazing, boundless, without beginning — which no one but you has ever seen before.
N: The chapter's resolution begins: Kṛṣṇa explains that the vision (rūpam ... darśitam, 'the form has been shown') came through ātma-yogāt, 'my own [power of] yoga' — an unearned gift to Arjuna, not something he attained himself. Ātma-yoga here names Kṛṣṇa's own supernatural capacity, not the disciplined practice yoga usually names elsewhere in the poem. Sandhi: तवार्जुनेदं packs tava + arjuna (a + a → ā) + arjuna + idam (a + i → e); यन्मे is yat + me (-t + m- → -n m-, the same assimilation as tat me → tan me at 1.46).
#48
L: Not by study-of-the-Vedas-and-sacrifice, not by gifts, not by rituals, not by fierce austerities, of such a form am I able, in the world of men, to be seen by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus.
I: Not by studying the Vedas or by sacrifice, not by giving gifts, not by rites, not by the fiercest austerities can I, in such a form, be seen in the world of men by anyone but you, mighty hero of the Kurus.
N: This verse spans the printed page: the Wikisource line ends दानै- and the next begins र्न, splitting the single sandhi-word dānaiḥ + na ('by gifts' + 'not') across the pāda break, exactly as sura-indra-loka- / m aśnanti was split at ch09 v.20; the entries here follow that precedent, tiling the source exactly and dividing the reading across the two tokens (dānai- / r na), the visarga of dānaiḥ surfacing as -r- before the voiced n- of na (-aiḥ + n- → -air n-), the same pattern as this verse's own vedayajñādhyayanair na and kriyābhir na. The verse repeats na four times, once before each instrumental (veda-yajña-adhyayanaiḥ, dānaiḥ, kriyābhiḥ, tapobhiḥ) — a standard anaphora of negation. Śakyaḥ ... draṣṭum is a gerundive-plus-infinitive construction, 'is able to be seen'; here and again in v.54, śakya's own visarga drops before the following aham without the usual guṇa to -o (contrast samo 'ham at 9.29) — an epic-Sanskrit metrical variant, not the regular rule.
#49
L: Let there not be fear of yours, nor confusion, at having seen this terrible form of mine, such as this; fear gone, mind glad, again you — that very form of mine, this, behold!
I: Do not be afraid, and do not be bewildered at having seen this terrible form of mine. Be free of fear again, your mind at ease: look, here is that same form of mine once more.
N: Mā with an understood verb of being is the standard Sanskrit prohibitive: te vyathā mā [bhūt], 'let there not be fear of yours'. Vimūḍha-bhāva and vyapeta-bhīḥ / prīta-manāḥ are bahuvrīhi compounds naming Arjuna's state, first terrified and then restored. Sandhi: विमूढभावो is vimūḍha-bhāvaḥ, -aḥ before d- → -o; घोरमीदृङ्ममेदम् packs ghoram + īdṛś (the stem's -ś reverting to its velar allomorph -k, then assimilating to -ṅ before the nasal m- of mama) + mama + idam (a + i → e); पुनस्त्वं is punaḥ + tvam (-aḥ + t- → -as t-, as in duryodhanas tadā at 1.2); तदेव is tat + eva (-t + e- → -d e-).
#50
L: Thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva having so spoken, his own form he displayed again; and comforted him, frightened, having become again gentle-bodied, the great-souled one.
I: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form once more, and comforted him in his fright, becoming again the great-souled one of gentle body.
N: The narrator's voice returns to close the theophany, as it did at the end of chapter 1. Vāsudeva, 'son of Vasudeva', is Kṛṣṇa's patronymic. Darśayāmāsa and āśvāsayāmāsa are both periphrastic perfects (root + -ām + āsa 'did'), the regular way Sanskrit forms the perfect tense of causative verbs. Saumya-vapuḥ mahātmā, 'gentle-bodied, great-souled', marks Kṛṣṇa's return to his familiar human form after the terrifying cosmic one. Sandhi: इत्यर्जुनं is iti + arjunam (-i + a- → -y a-); वासुदेवस्तथोक्त्वा packs vāsudevaḥ + tathā (-aḥ + t- → -as t-) + tathā + uktvā (ā + u → o); सौम्यवपुर्महात्मा is saumya-vapuḥ + mahā-ātmā (-uḥ + m- → -ur m-, the same visarga sandhi as before a vowel, e.g. yajur eva at 9.17, here before a voiced consonant instead).
#51
L: Having seen this human form of yours, gentle, O rouser-of-men, now I am become composed-minded, returned to [my own] nature.
I: Arjuna said: Seeing this human form of yours again, gentle Janārdana, I have come back to myself; my mind is calm, and I am restored to my own nature.
N: The meter returns here to the two-line anuṣṭubh/śloka that carries the rest of the poem, after the four-line triṣṭubh of verses 47-50 that marked the theophany's high point. Saṃvṛttaḥ ... prakṛtim gataḥ, 'become ... gone to [my own] nature', echoes language used elsewhere in the poem for cosmic dissolution and return, now applied to Arjuna's return to himself. Sandhi: दृष्ट्वेदं is dṛṣṭvā + idam (ā + i → e); इदानीमस्मि is idānīm + asmi, joined without change.
#52
L: Very-hard-to-see is this form which of mine you have seen; the gods too, of this form, always, are longing-to-see.
I: The Blessed Lord said: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to see; even the gods are forever longing to behold it.
N: Kṛṣṇa begins the chapter's closing teaching on how the cosmic form is, and is not, to be reached. Su-durdarśam stacks two prefixes on darśa 'sight' — su- intensifying, dur- 'hard' — for 'extremely hard to see'. Dṛṣṭavān asi is a periphrastic perfect, 'you have seen' (participle dṛṣṭavān + auxiliary asi), repeated in the next verse. Sandhi: सुदुर्दर्शमिदं is su-durdarśam + idam, joined without change; यन्मम is yat + mama (-t + m- → -n m-, as in yan me at v.47); देवा अप्यस्य is devāḥ + api (an -āḥ ending simply loses its visarga before any vowel, with no merger, unlike the -aḥ-before-a rule seen with śakya in v.48) + api + asya (-i + a- → -y a-).
#53
L: Not I by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by gift-giving, and not by sacrifice; able, of such a kind, to be seen, as you have seen me.
I: Not by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by giving, and not by sacrifice can I be seen — only as you have seen me.
N: This verse restates verse 48's fourfold denial from the far side of the vision, now naming ijyā 'sacrifice, worship' in place of that verse's kriyā 'ritual act'. Evaṃvidhaḥ draṣṭum, 'to be seen in such a manner', picks up evaṃrūpaḥ ... draṣṭum from v.48 almost word for word. Sandhi: नाहं is na + aham (a + a → ā); वेदैर्न is vedaiḥ + na (-aiḥ + n- → -air n-, as in veda-yajña-adhyayanaiḥ na at v.48); चेज्यया is ca + ijyayā (a + i → e); in शक्य एवंविधो, śakyaḥ's visarga drops regularly before the vowel e- of evaṃvidhaḥ — the ordinary rule for -aḥ before a non-a vowel, unlike the anomalous śakya aham of v.48 and v.54.
#54
L: By devotion, but, undivided, able am I, of such a kind, Arjuna, to be known, and to be seen in [my true] reality, and to be entered, O scorcher of the foe.
I: But through devotion that turns nowhere else, Arjuna, I can, in such a form, be known and seen in truth and entered into, scorcher of the foe.
N: The chapter's answer to its own riddle: what the Vedas, austerity, gift-giving and sacrifice cannot reach, ananyayā bhaktyā, 'undivided devotion', does. Bhakti is translated here as 'devotion' rather than left untranslated, since it is not on conventions.md's list of untranslated terms (dharma, yoga, brahman, the guṇas, sāṃkhya) — a choice worth revisiting once ch.12, named for it (Bhaktiyoga), is reached. Three infinitives share the one śakya: jñātum 'to know', draṣṭum 'to see', praveṣṭum 'to enter'. Sandhi: त्वनन्यया is tu + ananyayā (u + a → va, yaṇ sandhi); अहमेवंविधोऽर्जुन packs aham + evaṃvidhaḥ (joined without change) + evaṃvidhaḥ + arjuna (-aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha, the regular pattern — unlike śakya's own irregular elision earlier in the same line).
#55
L: My-work-doing, me-as-highest, my devotee, attachment-free; without hostility toward all beings — who, he comes to me, O son of Pāṇḍu.
I: One who does my work, holds me as the highest goal, is devoted to me, free of attachment, and without hostility toward any being — that one comes to me, Pāṇḍava.
N: The chapter's summary teaching and its closing verse, echoing the four-part formula of 9.34 (man-manāḥ, mad-bhaktaḥ...) but built here as a single relative-correlative sentence (yaḥ ... saḥ, 'who ... he') and ending, as ch.9 does, on the promise of reaching Kṛṣṇa. Bhakti/bhakta are again translated ('devotee') rather than left as bare Sanskrit, matching v.54 and ch.9's practice throughout. Sandhi: मत्कर्मकृन्मत्परमो packs mat-karma-kṛt (mad devoicing to mat- before the voiceless k-, a pattern new in this chapter; contrast mad-bhaktaḥ just after, where mad stays voiced before the voiced bh-) + mat-paramaḥ (kṛt + mat-: -t + m- → -n m-) + mat-paramaḥ + mad-bhaktaḥ (-aḥ before m- → -o); स is saḥ with its visarga dropped before the following consonant, the same pronoun-specific exception already seen at 1.13's sa ghoṣaḥ and 1.19's sa śabdaḥ — saḥ and eṣaḥ drop the visarga before any consonant, not only voiced ones.
